transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-08-21 15:00 PDT | Duration: 46 minutes | Recording: yes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Samir (Redwood CSM) — Lena, Marcus, Jia, Connor (StratusAI)

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're going to focus today on scoping the POC, specifically the cost/unit economics and the benchmark plan. Quick round of intros?
[00:10] Lena Torres: Hey, I'm Lena, Head of ML at Stratus. We're building a customer-assist chat that uses retrieval + LLMs for multi-turn support. Our main concerns: predictable latency under 200ms 95th, and staying inside a tight budget for initial pilot.
[00:25] Marcus Iqbal: Marcus here, infra lead. We run on GCP, VPC peering will be required, and we have strict egress rules.
[00:33] Jia Park: Jia, product. Success = better deflection and a clear cost per ticket metric.
[00:40] Priya Raman: Hi all, Priya (SE). I'll drive the benchmark harness and help size capacity. Before we jump in, can you confirm current traffic profile?
[00:49] Lena Torres: Sure, over the last month avg QPS is 8, spikes to 60 during business hours, average multi-turn session length 3.5 turns, avg tokens per request — we estimate ~420 tokens total (prompt+response), but we'll send logs.
[01:10] Priya Raman: Great. For cost modeling we usually start with per-1M token numbers. Quick rule of thumb we use in early scoping: hosted model baseline (non-quantized) runs around $30 per 1M tokens. With batching, prefix/KV cache and a quantized instance you can get down to the $6–12 / 1M token range depending on hit rates and latency SLOs.
[01:35] Marcus Iqbal: Could you break that down? $30 -> $6 is a big swing. What's the lever?
[01:41] Priya Raman: Yeah, so there's three primary levers: batching (amortizes kernel launch + scheduler cost), KV/prefix caching (eliminates repeated encoder cost for common context), and model quantization/compression which reduces GPU time. Example: if you have a 60% cache hit rate on the prefix (common for templated prompts), you avoid decoding the same prefix tokens 60% of the time. That combined with continuous batching for bursty traffic can reduce per-token GPU time substantially.
[02:10] Lena Torres: Our probes are fairly templated; we might be able to hit 50–70% prefix reuse. But question — how does that affect latency? We can't sacrifice the <200ms 95th.
[02:20] Priya Raman: Good question. There is a tradeoff. Continuous batching improves throughput and cost but can increase median latency slightly. Redwood's runtime supports latency-aware batching where small micro-batches are prioritized to meet tight SLOs and larger batching for lower-priority traffic. For a 200ms 95th SLO, we'd likely configure small max batch sizes and aggressive cache use; that keeps latency within range while still gaining some batching efficiency.
[02:50] Alex Chen: To make this concrete — if your avg request is 420 tokens and we use baseline per-1M token $30, cost per request is roughly 0.0126 USD (420 * $30 / 1,000,000 = $0.0126). With an optimized stack (cache hit 60% + batching and quantized model) where per-1M token is $9, that same request becomes 0.00378 USD — so you go from 1.26 cents to ~0.38 cents per request.
[03:25] Jia Park: Those are helpful ballpark numbers. Can you run a quick example for concurrency requirements? If we want to support 60 RPS peak with 420 tokens avg, what capacity should we be thinking about?
[03:35] Priya Raman: Sure — ballpark: 60 RPS * 420 tokens = 25,200 tokens/sec. Multiply by 3600 = ~90.7M tokens/hour. For cost projection multiply tokens by per-1M token price. If hosted $30/1M -> hourly token cost = 90.7 * $30 = ~$2,721 / hour which sounds high because that's raw generation cost; in practice you'll see lower because of caching and concurrency amortization. If optimized to $9/1M it's ~$816 / hour. These are stress numbers; POC should establish realistic effective token counts and cache hit rates.
[04:20] Marcus Iqbal: Wait, that hourly looks huge — are those numbers typical?
[04:25] Priya Raman: They scale quickly with RPS and token length. Many customers optimize prompts and use retrieval to reduce generated tokens. Also note that those numbers are pure per-token compute cost and don't include commitments or reserved capacity discounts which change economics for Dedicated.
[04:40] Alex Chen: For Dedicated we usually model a committed monthly spend that maps to a throughput envelope. For your shape, a small dedicated pool might be in the $8–15k/month range depending on GPUs and availability, and that translates to per-1M token effective cost often below $6 once fully utilized. The tradeoff is commitment and predictability.
[05:02] Lena Torres: Understood. For the pilot we want to avoid big commitments. So we expect hosted first — baseline tests — then if numbers look good consider dedicated.
[05:10] Priya Raman: Makes sense. For the POC I'd propose the following benchmark plan: week 0 (prep) - instrument traces and provide canonical prompts; week 1 (baseline hosted run) - run steady-state and burst tests, measure latency percentiles and raw token cost; week 2 (cache + batching experiments) - tune cache key strategy and batching policies; week 3 (quantized model and dedicated sizing run) - test a quantized variant and forecast Dedicated pricing; week 4 - results, econ model, and go/no-go.
[05:45] Jia Park: Timeline looks good. What exact benchmarks will you run in week 1?
[05:50] Priya Raman: Baseline: 1) steady-state at avg QPS, 2) peak burst to 60 RPS, 3) tail-latency test, 4) variability with cold cache vs warmed cache. We'll capture token counts, latency percentiles, GPU utilization, and cost per-1M tokens. We'll also run a small A/B on prompt compression to see savings.
[06:15] Connor Lee: On the VPC side — we need guidance on network egress and VPC peering. Also interested in where logs/audits live for compliance.
[06:25] Alex Chen: For Private/Dedicated we support VPC peering and customer-managed networking; logs can be pushed to your SIEM and audit events are available. We'll share our security whitepaper (SOC2 and audit log details).
[06:40] Marcus Iqbal: Great. Back to numbers — can you give a more granular per-1M token sheet for hosted options (standard, batch-optimized, quantized) so we can plug into our product metrics?
[06:50] Priya Raman: Yes, we'll send a cost sheet. Off the cuff: hosted standard non-quant $30/1M, hosted with batching & prefix cache tuned $12/1M, hosted quantized variant $9/1M. Dedicated effective cost if committed and fully utilized: $4–6/1M. These are illustrative — POC will produce actual measured points.
[07:10] Lena Torres: Are there additional hidden costs like tokenization overhead, network egress, or storage for KV cache?
[07:16] Priya Raman: Tokenization compute is usually negligible relative to decoding cost, but it is accounted for. Network egress depends on where you deploy — hosted within region has minimal egress, but cross-region will add. For KV/prefix cache we recommend inline memory-backed caches on the infer nodes; storage costs are small compared to compute but we'll quantify in the runbook.
[07:40] Jia Park: For the POC quality criteria — we want: 95th <200ms, cost per ticket < $0.02, and maintain F1 on our classification >= existing baseline. Can you map those to the plan?
[07:53] Priya Raman: Absolutely. During week 1 we'll measure current model F1 and latency. Week 2 optimizations target the latency and cost per ticket. We can set automated regression checks tied to your evaluation prompts. If the cost per ticket can't be reached on hosted, we'll model Dedicated as the follow-up.
[08:15] Marcus Iqbal: About evaluation prompts — we'll provide three canonical reward-shaped prompts: short policy clarifications (~150 tokens), medium troubleshooting flow (~450 tokens), and long diagnostic (~900 tokens). How will that affect the bench?
[08:27] Priya Raman: That distribution is perfect. We'll run a blended workload with those proportions to get realistic tail behavior. The long diagnostic will exercise KV cache less (less repetition) so it'll show worst-case cost.
[08:45] Alex Chen: Quick call-out on caching strategy: prefix caching helps where initial context is repeated (like plugin prompts or company policies). For multi-turn retrieval, chunking and dedup of retrieved docs can materially lower tokens sent. We'll include recommendations for retrieval chunk size and dedup heuristics in the runbook.
[09:05] Lena Torres: Cool. Any notes on tool-calling or function calls? We will call internal systems on some flows which adds round-trips.
[09:12] Priya Raman: We support structured outputs and tool calling. Each call itself is an extra prompt/response pair — you'll want to factor those tokens into per-ticket economics. If you can aggregate tool calls or batch them before the generation step you reduce token churn. We'll model that in the harness if you give examples.
[09:35] (Background: muted chatter)
[09:40] Marcus Iqbal: Real quick — what's the expected POC cost to Redwood for running these benchmarks? We need that number to evaluate organizational buy-in.
[09:48] Alex Chen: Typically the POC runs are lightweight; we'll estimate a few hundred to low-thousand dollars in compute depending on test intensity. We'll include an estimate in the kickoff docs.
[09:58] Jia Park: Ok. On the data side — any concerns about sending anonymized logs and prompts?
[10:05] Samir Patel: We recommended removing any PII before uploading; we also support a private deployment path if you prefer not to send logs to hosted. For the POC, anonymized traces are fine and standard.
[10:20] Priya Raman: One more technical detail: cold starts matter for tail latency. We'll run warm-up routines and include real-world cold-start tests. For batching micro-windows we typically use a 5–10ms wait bound for low-latency SLOs.
[10:40] Lena Torres: Good to know. Next — what artifacts will you send right after this call?
[10:45] Alex Chen: We'll send: 1) benchmark harness repo and runbook, 2) illustrative cost sheet (hosted/dedicated breakouts), 3) security whitepaper link, 4) proposed POC kickoff calendar invite. Expect those within 48 hours.
[10:59] Marcus Iqbal: Sounds good. Any blockers from Redwood side?
[11:03] Priya Raman: None — just need the logs and prompts from you and network contact for VPC peering if we later go to Dedicated.
[11:12] Lena Torres: We'll aim to share logs by Sunday and lock kickoff on 26th.
[11:18] Alex Chen: Perfect. Quick recap of measurable success criteria for the POC: 95th latency <200ms for at least 90% of blended workload, cost per ticket below $0.02 across the blended workload, and no regression on your F1 metric. Also produce an econ sheet mapping host vs dedicated breakeven points.
[11:40] Jia Park: Agreed. Anything else?
[11:43] Priya Raman: I'll mention instrumentation — please add request IDs to traces and capture full token counts (input/output) so the harness can report accurate per-request cost.
[11:55] Lena Torres: Will do. Thanks everyone.
[11:58] Alex Chen: Thanks, we'll follow up with artifacts and a calendar invite. Meeting end.
